title: Cookies and Browser State Security
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Cookies and Browser State Security.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Cookies and Browser State Security and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Cookies and Browser State Security, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 6: HTTP, Browser Boundaries, and Transport Security. It builds practical understanding of Cookies and Browser State Security with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Cookies and Browser State Security helps you observe a real boundary instead of assuming that browser, proxy, transport, and server behavior are interchangeable. Validate identity with a reviewed authentication design, protect session/token lifecycle and recovery, enforce server-side authorization separately, and test expiry, revocation, and failure paths.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Cookies and Browser State Security can be understood through this sequence: Establish identity → Protect credential → Manage token/session → Test expiry + recovery. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 44.1 Cookie scope and lifetime; 44.2 Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes; 44.3 Host-bound cookie prefixes; 44.4 Cookie domain and path considerations; 44.5 Browser storage versus server-managed state. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Validate identity with a reviewed authentication design, protect session/token lifecycle and recovery, enforce server-side authorization separately, and test expiry, revocation, and failure paths.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Cookies and Browser State Security
content_blocks.code:
response.set_cookie(
    key="session",
    value=cryptographically_random_session_id,
    httponly=True,
    secure=True,
    samesite="lax",
    max_age=1800,
)
content_blocks.expected_output: Sets an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookie with a 30-minute maximum age. Use HTTPS and server-side expiration/revocation as well.
content_blocks.run_instructions: FastAPI/Starlette response example; `cryptographically_random_session_id` is a placeholder for a generated opaque session ID, not a literal secret.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Validate identity with a reviewed authentication design, protect session/token lifecycle and recovery, enforce server-side authorization separately, and test expiry, revocation, and failure paths. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Cookies and Browser State Security”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Cookies and Browser State Security in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Cookies and Browser State Security is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Validate identity with a reviewed authentication design, protect session/token lifecycle and recovery, enforce server-side authorization separately, and test expiry, revocation, and failure paths.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
